common_name: Our Dorothy Louisiana Iris (Multicolor Brick-Pink Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in a sunny, constantly moist bed or pond margin so the clump is established before the mid-to-late spring bloom flush.

directions: Our Dorothy carries a multicolor blend of brick red, pink, and orange tones on each fall, centered on a bright yellow arrow-shaped signal, with color deepening toward pink as the bloom ages. It flowers over a roughly two-week window in mid-to-late spring and holds up well in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Give it full sun and soil that never fully dries out, since like other Louisiana iris cultivars it is adapted to swampy, slightly acidic ground. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor and flower count.

common_name: Bayou Comus Louisiana Iris (Historic Light Tan Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in consistently damp, humus-rich soil so the clump can root in ahead of its midseason-to-late bloom the following spring.

directions: Bayou Comus is an older Louisiana iris selection grown for its uniform light tan self coloring, a soft, unusual shade among the more commonly red, blue, and purple-toned hybrids in this group. It blooms midseason to late in the Louisiana iris season, extending garden color after many earlier cultivars have finished. As with other members of the group, it wants full sun and soil that stays wet to consistently moist, performing especially well at pond edges or in rain garden low spots. Lift and divide the clump every few years once flowering declines to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Birdland Louisiana Iris (Baby Blue Ruffled Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Install rhizome divisions in fall at the edge of a pond or in a reliably moist border bed to support strong early-to-midseason bloom the following spring.

directions: Birdland produces soft baby-blue standards and falls, with lavender-tinted style arms and a yellow signal that brightens toward the base of each fall. It is on the shorter side for a Louisiana iris cultivar, making it useful toward the front of a bog bed or along a shallow pond shelf where taller hybrids would block the view. It flowers in the early-to-midseason window and prefers full sun with soil that is kept constantly moist to wet. Divide crowded clumps after bloom every few years to keep flowering strong.
sources: Garden Club of Houston Bulb & Plant Mart

common_name: Moon Pie Louisiana Iris (Fragrant Yellow-Orange Veined Iris)

planting.note: Set divisions in fall in full sun and wet to constantly moist soil to establish roots before the midseason bloom the following spring.

directions: Moon Pie opens light yellow-orange flowers marked with fine violet veining on the standards and bolder violet veining on the falls, each fall centered on a large orange-yellow arrow signal, and carries a light spicy fragrance that is unusual among Louisiana iris hybrids. It blooms midseason and performs best in full sun with soil that stays wet to consistently moist, matching the needs of its wild Gulf Coast parent species. Use it at a pond margin or in a rain garden low spot where other perennials would struggle with standing water. Divide the clump every several years as vigor and bloom count decline.
sources: Garden Club of Houston Bulb & Plant Mart

common_name: Dorothea K. Williamson Louisiana Iris (Historic Fragrant Blue-Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil so the clump has a season to root in before its late-spring bloom.

directions: Dorothea K. Williamson is one of the earliest named Louisiana iris hybrids still grown today, bearing velvety blue-purple flowers marked with a yellow line signal and a noticeably strong, pleasant fragrance that sets it apart from most Louisiana iris cultivars. Its hybrid origin gives it good cold tolerance for the group, letting northern growers succeed with it in bog gardens where straight species parents would struggle. It blooms late in the Louisiana iris season and wants full sun with soil that is kept consistently wet, doing well at pond edges or in a dedicated bog bed. Established clumps benefit from division every several years to refresh vigor and bloom production.

common_name: Arabian Bayou Louisiana Iris (Cream-Peach Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Install rhizome divisions in fall at a shallow pond margin or wet bed so roots establish ahead of late-spring-to-early-summer bloom.

directions: Arabian Bayou produces large, softly colored flowers in cream to peach tones with a narrow gold crest on the falls and a green throat, giving it a gentler look than the brighter reds and blues common in the group. It flowers in late spring to early summer and forms upright, sword-leaved clumps typical of Louisiana iris hybrids. Grow it in full sun in soil that stays wet to constantly moist, such as a shallow pond shelf or low rain garden spot, since it does not tolerate drying out between waterings. Divide congested clumps every few years after bloom to maintain flower production.
